explanation: Numerical precision is how finely a value is represented. Quantization stores values using a more compact representation, reducing weight memory and sometimes accelerating supported computation.
Storage precision and compute precision can differ. A four-bit model is not necessarily performing every operation in four bits. Lower precision may damage some capabilities more than others.
mechanism: Precision describes how numerical values are represented. FP32 uses more bits than FP16 or BF16; FP16 and BF16 both use 16 bits but allocate range and precision differently. INT8 and 4-bit schemes represent values more compactly, often using scales and other metadata.

Storage precision and compute precision can differ. A runtime may store compressed weights and convert blocks into a higher precision for operations. Mixed precision uses different representations in different parts of the workload. Quality and speed effects depend on the model and supported kernels.
example: A laptop cannot load a full-precision model comfortably.
A supported quantized build reduces the weight footprint, leaving room for the cache. The user retests extraction accuracy and latency rather than assuming no behavior changed.
A small memory reduction with a large quality loss would be a poor trade for that task.
use: Use precision choices to fit resource constraints, guided by measured quality and hardware support.
caution: A 4-bit label does not mean every value, activation, cache entry, or operation in the system uses four bits.
question: Why can a quantized model occupy more than the naive weight-bit estimate?
answer: Scales, metadata, unquantized layers, runtime allocations, and caches add overhead beyond the packed weight values.
title: Precision without the maths
scope: FP32, FP16, BF16, INT8, 4-bit representations, storage versus compute precision, mixed precision, and quality/resource tradeoffs.

explanation: Post-training quantization transforms an already trained model. Quantization-aware training incorporates the effects of lower precision during training. Calibration examples can help select representations that preserve important behavior.
Weights, activations, and the KV cache can be quantized separately. The choice affects different memory costs. Always evaluate the configuration you will actually deploy.
mechanism: Post-training quantization converts an already trained model. Quantization-aware training includes simulated or actual quantization effects during training so parameters can adapt. Methods may compress weights, activations, or the KV cache; these affect different parts of memory and execution.

Calibration uses representative inputs to estimate useful ranges or sensitivities. Outliers are unusually large values that can make a single shared range waste precision. Per-channel or grouped schemes assign finer-grained scales, trading metadata and implementation complexity for fidelity.
example: A team calibrates a document model only on short English prose.
It then evaluates long code snippets and another language, where errors increase. The calibration examples did not represent deployment well.
The team improves coverage and compares quality before accepting the quantized release.
use: Pick methods supported by your runtime, then test the actual task distribution. Distinguish weight-memory savings from cache-memory savings.
caution: Quantization is a family of methods, not one uniform conversion with a guaranteed quality cost.
question: Would quantizing only the KV cache shrink the downloaded weight files?
answer: No. It targets request-time cache storage. Weight-file compression requires a weight quantization or other model-storage change.
title: Quantization approaches
scope: Post-training quantization versus quantization-aware training; weight, activation, and KV-cache quantization; calibration data; outliers; per-channel/group choices at a conceptual level.

explanation: Labels such as a GGUF quantization variant, GPTQ, AWQ, or NF4 describe different representation and tooling choices. They are not interchangeable downloads for every engine.
Two four-bit artifacts can have different quality, memory overhead, and hardware kernels. Read the runtime's compatibility documentation and benchmark the actual combination.
mechanism: A quantization label describes an artifact or method within an ecosystem. GGUF labels can indicate bit families and mixed treatment of tensors. GPTQ and AWQ are weight-quantization approaches with their own conversion and runtime requirements. Bitsandbytes supports low-bit loading and training workflows; NF4 is a particular four-bit representation.

Equal nominal bit counts do not imply identical effective file size, calibration, numerical error, or speed. Read the artifact's description and compatible loader rather than treating every ‘4-bit’ file as interchangeable.
example: You download a four-bit checkpoint intended for one serving engine.
A different local runtime rejects it even though that runtime also advertises four-bit support. The packaging, architecture, or kernels are incompatible.
You select an artifact explicitly supported by the runtime and repeat the baseline tests.
use: Record the complete filename, quantization method, base revision, and runtime version when sharing results or troubleshooting.
caution: Do not infer a universal quality ranking from a filename suffix. Compare task results for the actual artifacts.
question: Can you rename a quantized file's extension to convert it?
answer: No. Conversion changes tensor representation and metadata. Renaming changes only the label on the file, not its contents.
title: Reading quantized model labels
scope: GGUF quantization labels, GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes/NF4 as ecosystem examples; runtime and hardware compatibility; why equal bit counts do not imply equal quality or speed.

explanation: Distillation trains a student model using guidance from another model. Pruning removes selected parameters or structures. Sparsity means some values or operations can be omitted. Quantization changes precision.
These methods can be combined, but compression does not automatically produce acceleration. Hardware and software must exploit the changed representation.
mechanism: Distillation trains a student to imitate useful behavior from a teacher, using outputs, distributions, or representations. Pruning removes selected parameters or structures. Sparsity means many values or connections are absent or zero, but speedups require implementations that exploit that pattern.

Architectural changes can reduce repeated work or alter model capacity. A smaller checkpoint can still incur expensive operations, and an unstructured sparse model may run through dense kernels without a speed benefit. Evaluate memory, latency, and task quality separately.
example: A company distills a large support model into a smaller specialist.
The student handles common routing cases quickly but struggles with unusual multi-issue tickets. A held-out set reveals the gap.
The product routes uncertain cases to a stronger model or human instead of assuming imitation preserved every capability.
use: Use compression when a defined task must meet device, latency, or cost constraints. Keep difficult and rare cases in evaluation.
caution: A student does not automatically inherit all the teacher's knowledge or reliability, and it can inherit the teacher's mistakes.
question: Why might pruning half the weights fail to halve response time?
answer: The runtime may still perform dense operations, or memory transfers and other components may dominate. Hardware-aware structure and measurement matter.
title: Compression beyond quantization
scope: Distillation, pruning, sparsity, and architectural changes; checkpoint size versus runtime memory; why 'smaller' and 'faster' are separate claims.
